content: Every year, a significant number of needles and syringes are not disposed of safely, posing risks of injury and infection while also missing opportunities for reuse. Unsafe disposal practices contribute to approximately 7 million hepatitis B infections and 315,000 hepatitis C infections annually. Additional dangers arise from scavenging at unsecured waste disposal sites and manually handling hazardous healthcare waste, practices that are particularly common in lowand middle-income countries. In 2015, a joint assessment by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF revealed that only 58% of healthcare facilities in 24 countries had adequate systems for the safe disposal of healthcare waste. To mitigate the unintended harmful effects of self-care products on human health and the environment, it is essential to procure environmentally friendly (or green) goods while maintaining clinical outcomes. WHO adheres to a green procurement policy, prioritizing goods and services that minimize environmental impact during production, use, and disposal, whenever feasible and cost-effective. Environmental considerations, such as energy consumption, toxicity, ozone depletion, and radiation, must be evaluated before finalizing procurement decisions. Environmentally preferable purchasing involves selecting products and services with the least environmental damage, ranging from recycled paper to medical equipment assessed for its life-cycle environmental impact. WHO supports the safe and sustainable management of healthcare waste and recommends that countries conduct assessments to identify appropriate waste management methods. Tools are available to assist in this decision-making process, ensuring that policies lead to the adoption of suitable technologies. WHO's core principles emphasize that all healthcare financing and support must include provisions for managing healthcare waste, as this is a duty of care. Manufacturers also bear responsibility for considering waste management in the development and sale of their products and services. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Health Care Without Harm launched the Sustainable Health in Procurement Project (SHiPP) in 2018 to reduce harm to people and the environment caused by the production, use, and disposal of medical products. Under the UNDP's procurement strategy, initiatives such as sustainability assessments of long-term suppliers of antiretrovirals have been implemented. These assessments consider international standards and reporting systems to evaluate suppliers' environmental impact. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the volume of medical waste, particularly plastic personal protective equipment (PPE), increased significantly. For example, hospitals in Wuhan, China, produced over six times more waste than usual during the outbreak's peak. The safe disposal of such waste is critical not only to prevent further virus transmission but also to mitigate environmental harm, such as the release of microplastic fibers from face masks. These challenges highlight the need for further research and policy changes in solid waste management. Educational initiatives, such as UNICEF Romania's project during the pandemic, have raised awareness about the responsible disposal of used face masks and other self-care products. Tens of thousands of children in Romania have been educated on the importance of collecting these items in closed containers to prevent viral contamination and environmental pollution. Teachers and students have collaborated to create action plans promoting responsible waste collection and community awareness. WHO emphasizes the importance of integrating environmental considerations into healthcare waste management systems. Donors and partners should include provisions for waste management in their health program assistance, while non-governmental organizations should advocate for and implement programs that promote sound waste management. The private sector must also take responsibility for managing healthcare waste associated with their products and services, including through sustainable product design and packaging. In response to the growing use of self-care products, WHO recommends expanding research on self-care interventions to address gaps in evidence, particularly for underserved populations such as gender-diverse individuals. Research priorities should align with national and regional public health goals and focus on innovative self-care tools and interventions for populations affected by health emergencies. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO supported research to address global priorities and improve access to self-care interventions as part of its commitment to achieving universal health coverage and protecting populations from health threats.
